statement: An NP has a determiner and a head nominal; the hierarchy NP > nominal > noun parallels clause > VP > verb; modifiers and complements inside the nominal are internal dependents, while peripheral modifiers and predeterminers are external.

statement: An attributive modifier is an internal pre-head dependent in a nominal; it is most often an adjective, but can also be a nominal, a determinative or a verb or VP in gerund-participle or past participle form.

statement: The adjective is the head of an adjective phrase (AdjP), which is the single higher-level unit needed for adjectives; unlike nouns and verbs, adjectives have no subject or determiner function motivating a second higher-level category. AdjP dependents are modifiers or complements; complements follow the head and are usually PPs or clauses.
condition: Applies to adjective-headed phrases: analyse the adjective and its dependents as an AdjP; there is no further higher-level unit analogous to nominal/NP or VP/clause, since adjectives have no subject or determiner function. Modifiers precede the head; complements follow it and are usually PPs or clauses.

exceptions.description: Only one or two adjectives are transitive and can take an NP complement directly; the source names worth and like. Most adjective-related NPs are instead linked through a preposition.

correct.text: It was very good. [modifier]
He seems a bit grumpy. [modifier]
She is ashamed of him. [PP complement]
I'm glad you could come. [clause complement]
the minister responsible for the decision [complement in postpositive AdjP]
The old camera is worth a careful inspection.
correct.note: Worth takes a direct NP complement.

correct.text: The twins are very like each other.
correct.note: Like is one of the rare transitive adjectives identified in the source.

correct.text: She is fond of animals.
correct.note: The NP is linked to the adjective through a preposition.

review_notes: Hedges ('hardly permitted', 'minor exceptions') are preserved; do not turn into constraints without Ch. 6. Cambridge Ch. 6 §1, pp. 526–527, confirms the single AdjP level and explains that adjectives in be + adjective constructions provide the main semantic predicate. It also identifies worth and like as rare transitive adjectives; the ordinary pattern relates an NP to an adjective through a preposition.

statement: The adverb is the head of an adverb phrase (AdvP), the single higher-level unit needed for adverbs; AdvP can be expanded in ways that are broadly a subset of those available to AdjPs, in part because adverbs have no predicative function.
condition: Applies to adverb-headed phrases: analyse the adverb and its dependents as an AdvP; there is no further higher-level unit analogous to nominal/NP or VP/clause. Adverbs allow a narrower range of phrase expansion than adjectives, broadly a subset of AdjP options, and only a very small number license complements.

independently of such considerations

statement: In a PP the NP in 'to you' or 'of the house' is a complement of the preposition, and modifiers like 'a few minutes' or 'straight' before or after the preposition are modifiers; complements may be objects or predicatives (as a liability) and a PP may have no complement.

statement: The most central prepositions can be stranded, i.e. left with a gap in complement position, when their complement is prenuclear in an interrogative or relative clause; the alternative is to keep the PP together in prenuclear position.
